item.title: Meesho’s Next Monetisation Engines
item.dc:creator: Gargi Sarkar
item.description: Meesho has spent much of its journey building scale in India’s value commerce market. Its low-cost marketplace model has helped…
item.content:encoded:
Meesho has spent much of its journey building scale in India’s value commerce market. Its low-cost marketplace model has helped it expand its reach beyond large cities, bring more sellers online and attract consumers looking for affordable products. But as the company moves towards its next phase of growth, the goalpost is shifting from acquiring users and expanding transactions to extracting more value from the ecosystem it has built.

Advertising is emerging as one of the key opportunities. With 284 Mn annual transacting users (ATUs) and 1.13 Mn annual transacting sellers as of Q2 FY27, Meesho has a large marketplace that it can potentially monetise through sponsored listings and other advertising products. The company expects advertising to become a more meaningful contributor to its revenue mix from FY28.

At the same time, Meesho is exploring newer business lines, including lending products for consumers and sellers, while expanding branded commerce through Meesho Mall and discovery-led shopping through content commerce. These initiatives could open up additional revenue streams, although their contribution to the company’s financials remains at an early stage.

The opportunity comes as Meesho makes progress on its marketplace economics. 

Its Q2 FY27 performance shows that the core marketplace is growing and its operating economics are improving. Revenue from operations increased 34% year-on-year to ₹4,119.9 Cr, while net merchandise value (NMV) grew 23% to ₹12,911 Cr. 

In the reported quarter, its contribution margin improved to 6% of net merchandise value (NMV), compared with 4.6% in the previous quarter and 3.3% a year earlier. Its marketplace adjusted EBITDA loss also narrowed to ₹130.5 Cr from ₹371 Cr in Q2 FY26. 

However, management cautioned that the 6% contribution margin recorded in Q2 FY27 should not be viewed as the new normal, as some of the logistics efficiency gains may be passed on to consumers and sellers to support growth.

The question, therefore, is whether Meesho can turn its growing consumer and seller base into higher-value revenue streams without compromising the affordability that underpins its marketplace.

Advertising: Can Meesho Monetise Its Scale?

Advertising offers Meesho a way to generate more revenue from the traffic and transactions already flowing through its platform. As its user base and seller ecosystem expand, the company has an opportunity to charge sellers for better visibility and access to consumers who are actively browsing products.

For sellers, sponsored placements can help products stand out in a crowded marketplace. For Meesho, they can create an additional revenue stream without requiring it to take ownership of inventory or significantly change its core marketplace model. This is particularly relevant in a business where affordability and low prices remain central to customer acquisition.

The scale of the opportunity is supported by Meesho’s operating metrics. Its ATUs grew 21% year-on-year to 284 Mn in Q2 FY27, while annual transacting sellers increased 60% to 1.13 Mn. Placed orders rose 17% to 819 Mn during the quarter, and NMV grew 23% to ₹12,911 Cr.

“A larger marketplace gives Meesho more opportunities to connect seller advertising with consumer discovery. However, the size of its user base alone does not determine how much it can earn from ads. The company will need to demonstrate that sellers are willing to spend consistently on advertising and that paid placements generate measurable returns through product views and orders,” an ecommerce analyst said.

Advertising monetisation is still at a relatively early stage. On the Q2 FY27 earnings call, it said the sequential improvement in contribution margin was primarily driven by logistics efficiencies, rather than a significant increase in advertising monetisation. It also expects advertising to become a more meaningful contributor as a percentage of NMV in FY28.

Motilal Oswal expects higher advertising monetisation to support contribution margin expansion from FY28, citing seller demand for advertising and the potential to improve the platform’s monetisation.

However, Meesho will have to balance monetisation with the shopping experience. Its value-commerce positioning depends on offering consumers affordable products and a wide selection. If sponsored placements make discovery less relevant or push sellers towards higher advertising expenditure that is eventually reflected in product prices, the company could risk weakening some of the advantages of its model.

The other consideration is the distribution of advertising benefits across sellers. Larger and more established sellers may have greater capacity to spend on visibility, while smaller sellers could find it harder to compete for prominent placements. Meesho will need to build an advertising ecosystem that delivers returns for sellers across different sizes and categories, the analyst added..

The key monitorable, therefore, is not simply the growth in advertising revenue, but how much of that revenue Meesho can retain as incremental contribution after accounting for the cost of serving the marketplace. If advertising can scale without materially increasing operating costs or affecting affordability, it could become a more durable margin lever.

New Initiatives: Lending, Mall And Content Commerce 

Beyond advertising, Meesho is looking to deepen its engagement with consumers and sellers through a wider set of services. These initiatives could increase the number of ways in which the company earns from its ecosystem, although they are at different stages of development.

One area is lending. During the earnings call, management confirmed that Meesho is working on both consumer-side and seller-side lending products. The company is expanding its network of non-banking financial company (NBFC) partners and is also looking to work with banks.

For consumers, access to credit could potentially support purchases on the platform, while seller financing could help merchants manage working capital and grow their businesses. If structured effectively, these offerings could strengthen Meesho’s relationship with both sides of the marketplace.

However, the company has not disclosed lending-related assets under management, revenue targets or the expected financial contribution of these products. It is also not clear how much of the lending opportunity Meesho intends to capture directly versus through its lending partners. For now, it is better viewed as an emerging business opportunity than an established monetisation engine.

Meesho Mall and content commerce represent another route to deepen marketplace engagement. Meesho Mall, which had around 1,800 brands in Q2 FY27, recorded 81% YoY growth in NMV. NMV from Tier 3 and smaller markets grew 89%, while around half of Mall customers during the quarter were first-time buyers on the branded-commerce offering.

The growth indicates that Meesho is making progress in bringing branded products to a consumer base that has traditionally been associated with unbranded and lower-priced merchandise. A broader product mix could help the platform attract new customer segments and increase the range of purchases made by existing users.

Content commerce is also expanding. Its NMV grew 160% YoY in Q2 FY27, while the number of content pieces generating orders increased 144% to 2.2 Mn. The ecosystem had more than 4 lakh sellers participating in content-led commerce.

The proposition is to use videos and other content formats to help consumers discover products, rather than relying entirely on search-led shopping. This could create more product discovery opportunities and potentially improve engagement. Meesho has also said that the share of orders coming from discovery-led recommendations has increased, alongside time spent on the platform.

However, rapid growth from these offerings does not automatically translate into a meaningful revenue contribution. Meesho has not disclosed the share of total NMV generated by Mall or Content Commerce, nor has it provided specific monetisation targets for either. Their longer-term value will depend on whether they can increase purchase frequency, attract higher-value transactions and create additional opportunities for advertising.

AI is another part of this effort. Meesho is using AI across product discovery, ranking, fraud prevention and logistics, while also deploying AI agents in engineering and other internal functions. The company said 65% of its engineering pods were operating with one engineer directing AI agents. It reported a 41% reduction in code-review approval time and a reduction in data-science model deployment time from 17 days to three days.

These productivity gains could help the company develop products and improve operations faster. But AI also brings infrastructure costs. Meesho’s GPU footprint increased 150%, while server costs rose to 2.3% of NMV in Q2 FY27 from 1.9% in the previous quarter. Management expects these costs to normalise towards the previous baseline as a percentage of NMV by Q4 FY27, but that remains an expectation to be tested.

The newer initiatives are also still investment-heavy. Management has indicated that it is keeping investments in these businesses within a cap of around ₹200 Cr, while emphasising that product-market fit and unit economics will be important before scaling further. This suggests that Meesho is not yet positioning these offerings as immediate contributors to profitability.

The Profitability Test

The monetisation opportunity has to be seen alongside Meesho’s broader effort to improve its marketplace economics. The company reported a contribution margin of ₹775 Cr in Q2 FY27, up from ₹531 Cr in Q1 FY27. As a percentage of NMV, the margin improved to 6% from 4.6% sequentially.

The improvement was largely driven by lower logistics costs, supported by better order density, network redesign, improved route utilisation and efforts to reduce return-to-origin (RTO) orders. Management also indicated that it intends to recover some of the logistics-related margin spread lost in FY26 towards FY25 levels during FY27.

However, it has cautioned against extrapolating the Q2 contribution margin as the new normal. Some of the savings could be passed on to sellers and consumers through lower prices, while a part may be retained to improve profitability. The timing and extent of this balance will matter as Meesho enters the festive period and continues to invest in growth.

There are also costs that could absorb some of the gains. Meesho’s advertising and sales promotion expenses increased ahead of the festive season, taking growth spending to 2.9% of NMV in Q2 FY27 from 2.1% in Q1. Server costs also rose, reflecting the higher computing requirements of the platform.

The company reported a consolidated adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹172.1 Cr in Q2 FY27, while its consolidated net loss narrowed to ₹132.4 Cr from ₹411.4 Cr a year earlier. Although the marketplace business is moving towards better unit economics, its newer initiatives continue to add to the overall loss.

Cash flow also needs to be viewed over a longer period. Meesho reported positive consolidated free cash flow of ₹345 Cr in Q2 FY27, compared with an outflow of ₹226 Cr in Q1. But its last-twelve-month consolidated free cash flow remained negative at ₹565 Cr. The quarterly improvement was partly supported by seasonal working-capital movements, as collections from consumers ahead of the festive sale preceded settlements with sellers.

This makes the quality and durability of cash generation an important measure of progress. Advertising could help improve margins because it allows Meesho to monetise marketplace activity without taking on inventory. Lending and other initiatives may create additional revenue opportunities, but their economics will depend on partner arrangements, customer adoption and the cost of scaling.

Brokerage views reflect both the opportunity and the execution risks. Motilal Oswal sees advertising as a medium-term margin lever and expects contribution margins to remain well above FY26 levels. Nomura, however, has flagged the possibility of some margin improvement reversing in Q3 FY27 as the company reinvests gains into growth and category expansion during the festive season.

Ultimately, Meesho’s next phase will depend on how effectively it monetises the scale it has already built and whether new businesses can add revenue and improve customer and seller engagement without pushing up costs or weakening Meesho’s low-price proposition. For a platform that has built its position on affordability and scale, monetisation will have to deepen the business without changing what makes it attractive to consumers and sellers.

item.title: Netflix Flips Its India Script
item.dc:creator: Gargi Sarkar
item.description: What if Netflix’s next big hit in India is not an expensive scripted original, but a reality show with a…
item.content:encoded:
What if Netflix’s next big hit in India is not an expensive scripted original, but a reality show with a ready-made fan base? The streaming giant appears to be warming up to an idea it once seemed determined to move away from: television.

Netflix is increasingly turning to established television franchises, reality formats and non-fiction programming to reach a wider audience in India. Its recent content choices, including Lock Upp, The Great Indian Kapil Show and deals for MTV Hustle and MTV Roadies, point to that shift in India.

The change is significant for a platform that initially built its India proposition around premium, urban-focused originals and international programming. In the fourth quarter of 2021, Netflix cofounder and the then CEO Reed Hastings described India as a “frustrating” market. He also stated that the company had not managed to get its flywheel spinning here as it had in other major markets.

Nearly five years later, Netflix emerged stronger. In the July-September quarter of 2026, its India revenue grew 18% year-on-year (YoY) on a foreign-exchange-neutral basis, while viewing hours increased 24%. The company also recorded its largest-ever quarter of paid net additions in the country.

The growth was driven by a content lineup featuring Lock Upp, Netflix’s first daily reality series, as well as scripted titles such as Musafir Cafe and Operation Safed Sagar. Netflix said Lock Upp generated the highest viewing hours of any title on its platform in India, measured over the first 91 days.

So, was this simply a strong quarter or evidence of a more fundamental shift in Netflix’s India playbook? 

Netflix Looks Beyond Its Urban Comfort Zone

Netflix’s growing interest in reality television is becoming difficult to miss. The platform has even bought MTV Roadies to Netflix India in a deal worth around ₹18 Cr with JioStar, as per media reports. And the strategy is not limited to one show. 

Over the past year, non-fiction content has assumed greater importance in Netflix’s strategy. This is also part of a larger effort to move beyond its Tier I, urban-centric audience. 

According to an industry analyst at one of the Big Four consulting firms, if Netflix wants to deepen its penetration and crack the Indian market, it cannot continue catering largely to the same urban viewers. It needs formats and stories that resonate with audiences across smaller cities and towns as well.

Reality and unscripted formats could help bridge that gap. Lock Upp’s performance on Netflix offers an early indication of the format’s potential. 

Regional programming is another part of this effort. Netflix is working with local production houses and regional OTT players to deepen its presence in language markets. Netflix has partnered with Bengali streaming platform Hoichoi to bring its upcoming series to a wider audience. Under the two-year deal, the shows will premiere in Bengali on Hoichoi and also be available on Netflix in Hindi, Tamil and Telugu.

Going All In On Bollywood Blockbusters

Netflix has continued to expand its film catalogue by securing streaming rights to established Bollywood titles and major theatrical releases. Its partnership with Yash Raj Films (YRF), announced last year, is one example. 

The deal brought a curated selection of YRF films to Netflix in phases, including nine Shah Rukh Khan films such as Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge, Mohabbatein and Veer-Zaara, along with Salman Khan blockbusters Ek Tha Tiger, Sultan and Tiger Zinda Hai. The lineup also included classics such as Chandni and Silsila, and Ranveer Singh films including Band Baaja Baaraat and Gunday.

The strategy extends beyond catalogue licensing to recent theatrical releases. Netflix also picked up the streaming rights to Dhurandhar, which landed on the platform in January 2026 following its release in theatres. For its sequel, Dhurandhar: The Revenge, Netflix secured international streaming rights, while JioHotstar acquired the India rights. 

An Ormax Media analysis of 126 films that crossed one million domestic footfalls in 2025 found that Netflix held a 36% share of streaming rights across the titles, the highest among platforms. Its share in Hindi theatrical films stood at 57%, up from 50% in 2024. 

The Race To Grab Eyeballs Gets Fiercer

Netflix’s India strategy is taking shape against the backdrop of an increasingly crowded streaming market. According to JustWatch’s Q2 2026 report, Netflix and Amazon Prime Video were tied at the top, each accounting for 22% of measured consumer interest. 

Netflix is also seeing stronger traction on the ground. In Q3 2026, the company recorded its highest-ever quarterly paid net additions in India, crediting a strong local content slate and its first transaction-based loyalty bundle with Flipkart. The partnership gives Netflix another route to consumers beyond direct subscriptions, tapping into Flipkart’s existing commerce ecosystem.

Its competitors, meanwhile, are not sitting still. Amazon Prime Video is doubling down on Indian intellectual property, multilingual programming and established franchises, while also looking to take Indian stories to global audiences. At its 2026 content showcase, the platform unveiled nearly 55 Indian original series and films, with more than 100 projects in development or production.

JioHotstar, on the other hand, is banking on a combination of television content, live sports, originals and regional programming to hold on to its mass-market audience. In January 2026, it introduced monthly subscription plans across its Mobile, Super and Premium tiers, starting at ₹79, making access more flexible for smartphone viewers and connected-TV households.

Apple TV+ is also widening its distribution reach. After gaining four percentage points in JustWatch’s rankings over the past year, it has expanded its India offering through an iCloud+ subscription bundle that combines access to Apple TV and Apple Arcade with cloud storage.

But audience growth is only one part of the equation. 

Netflix’s financial performance in India offers another measure of its progress. Netflix Entertainment Services India LLP reported a 63% increase in net profit to ₹85 Cr in FY25, while revenue from operations grew 32% to ₹3,769 Cr, according to filings with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

The cost of that growth, however, remains significant. Total expenses rose 32% to ₹3,711 Cr during the year. Other expenses, which include content production, marketing and related operating costs, increased 35% to ₹3,616 Cr, while personnel costs declined to ₹88 Cr from ₹106 Cr.

With content and related operating expenses accounting for most of its cost base, the company will need to ensure that its investments in new formats, wider audiences and distribution partnerships translate into sustained revenue growth and stronger returns on content spending.

Can It Go Mass Without Losing Its Edge?

Netflix’s position in India’s content market also varies across language industries. The South Indian film market is more fragmented, with producers having multiple streaming platforms to sell their content to, giving them greater bargaining power. On the other hand, the Hindi film industry has become more dependent on Netflix, according to industry sources. 

For Netflix, however, the bigger challenge is balancing audience expansion with its premium content positioning. Its growing focus on reality shows, established television franchises and mass-market formats could help it reach viewers beyond its traditional urban audience. 

But moving too far towards familiar, broad-appeal programming also carries the risk of diluting the distinctive content proposition that helped build Netflix. The platform will need to widen its audience without losing the storytelling ambition and premium identity that set it apart from other streaming services. 

This tension was also evident when Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos questioned, on Nikhil Kamath’s podcast, whether the platform had introduced Sacred Games too early in its India journey. His remarks irked sections of India’s creative community, which raises concerns over whether Netflix’s evolving strategy could come at the cost of the creative ambition that defined its early India slate.

That balancing act will be central to Netflix’s next phase of growth in India. Reality shows and established television franchises can bring in viewers who may not have been drawn to its earlier slate of premium scripted originals. Regional partnerships can deepen its presence across language markets, while distribution tie-ups can make subscriptions more accessible. However, the early growth signals need to translate into sustained engagement and subscriber additions for the strategy to deliver lasting results.

One strong quarter, even with record paid net additions, does not necessarily mean Netflix has cracked India. The company continues to face competition from Prime Video and JioHotstar, alongside a growing number of platforms competing for viewers, content and production partnerships. Can Netflix turn its new mass-market appeal into a lasting winning formula without losing its DNA? 

[Edited by Shishir Parasher]

item.title: Here’s Why Doctors Are Betting On Docterz’s Hospital Management Software
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Running a clinic involves more than examining patients. Like any business, doctors also need to manage their schedules, patient records,…
item.content:encoded:
Running a clinic involves more than examining patients. Like any business, doctors also need to manage their schedules, patient records, billing, staff and follow-ups, leaving them with less time to focus on medical care.

Mumbai-based Docterz is building a platform to ease this administrative burden. Founded over a decade ago by practising paediatrician Dr Atish Laddad, the startup offers an integrated electronic medical records and clinic management platform for doctors, clinics and healthcare organisations. It aims to simplify day-to-day clinic operations while helping doctors deliver more accessible and affordable healthcare.

With AI opening up new possibilities for automating routine tasks and improving clinical workflows, Docterz is looking to deepen its technology offering for the medical community.

The healthtech startup has now raised ₹5 Cr from around 35 investors, nearly 60% of which, or close to ₹3 Cr, came from approximately 20 doctors who already use its platform. The investor group also includes Sugar Cosmetics’ Vineeta Singh and CaratLane’s Avnish Anand.

The fresh capital will be used to drive organic growth, explore acquisitions and develop practical AI-powered tools for doctors.

Bringing Clinical And Administrative Workflows Under One Roof

In essence, Docterz aims to reduce the administrative workload of running a clinic, allowing doctors to spend more time on patient care while giving them better control over their clinic’s operations.

From arranging appointments and maintaining records to then aiding in prescriptions, billing, the all-in-one clinic management platform helps doctors handle everything. For this, the platform trains AI based OS on doctors’ prescription patterns to simplify the process of recommendations.

It also provides easy-to-understand medical information that doctors can share with patients, alongside tools to manage vaccine inventory, track expiry dates and monitor the use of medical supplies.

On the patients side, Docterz offers a WhatsApp-based assistant to book appointments, check live clinic waiting times, access medical records and view appointment history without downloading a separate app.

Docterz’s Commercial Bet

The latest fundraise comes with an interesting investor mix. Nearly 60% of the capital has come from doctors who already use Docterz, making the round a bet by its own customer base on the startup’s future.

According to the startup, several of these doctors have used the platform for years. For instance, Dr Dhananjay Sangle, a paediatrician and one of the user-investors, said he had been using Docterz across his clinic’s paediatric and OB-GYN practices for several years.

The participation of existing users could give Docterz an advantage as it looks to expand within the medical community. However, scaling a healthcare software business will require it to convert this initial user trust into wider adoption across independent practitioners and healthcare organisations.

With its users also now present on its cap table, the startup’s next phase of growth will focus on three areas:

  • AI-enabled tools: Docterz plans to introduce practical AI capabilities to address everyday clinical and practice-management tasks, including documentation, administrative workflows and practice-data analysis.
  • Organic and inorganic expansion: The company intends to grow its existing business while exploring acquisitions and other inorganic opportunities.
  • Wider doctor adoption: Docterz plans to reach more independent practitioners and smaller clinics across India, while continuing to build its patient-engagement capabilities.

It also plans to strengthen integrations with India’s digital-health ecosystem, including the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM).

Inc42 Take: Can Docterz Become The Operating System For Doctors?

Docterz is targeting a fairly fundamental problem in healthcare.

An integrated platform could help reduce a doctor’s burden, particularly for independent practitioners and smaller clinics that may not have the resources to manage multiple systems.

The participation of around 20 existing doctor-users in the round is also an encouraging signal of product acceptance. However, user trust is only one part of building a scalable healthcare software business.

The larger challenge now is to get more doctors to move their existing records and workflows onto the platform. Once they are there, their retention also depends on whether the software can deliver tangible operational benefits.

AI could also open another avenue for growth, particularly across documentation, patient follow-ups and administrative tasks. 

The value of these tools will depend on how seamlessly they fit into doctors’ existing workflows and how responsibly patient information is handled.

item.title: ED Arrests Armstrong Exchange Founder Over Alleged Online Betting Scam
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has arrested Armstrong Exchange founder Sagar Dash in connection with an alleged online gaming and betting…
item.content:encoded:
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has arrested Armstrong Exchange founder Sagar Dash in connection with an alleged online gaming and betting scam.

In a statement, ED said that Dash was arrested on October 27 under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002. A special PMLA court in Mumbai has now remanded Dash to ED custody for three days.

The directorate said that the probe was initiated after three FIRs were filed in connection with online betting and cyber fraud involving All Panel Exchange (APX). Afterwards, the ED began probing the operations of APX and related financial transactions. 

The agency subsequently uncovered an alleged network of mule accounts and shell entities, which were used to route proceeds of crime worth hundreds of crores.

The agency alleged that Dash used fabricated documents and KYC details of an account, maintained on behalf of an entity called Armstrong Exchange Pvt Ltd and set up by Dash, with Nagarbhavi Credit Cooperative Society to open a cryptocurrency account. 

The ED further claimed that hundreds of crores were routed through the cooperative society’s bank account, with a substantial portion directly linked to proceeds generated through illegal gaming and betting platforms.

According to the ED, the proceeds of the crime were initially routed through multiple mule accounts maintained with Jubilee Hills Mercantile Cooperative Bank in Hyderabad. The money was then transferred to various shell entities, and significant amounts were moved to the aforementioned nodal account at Nagarbhavi Credit Cooperative Society in Bengaluru.

The ED said it is continuing its investigation in the matter to trace the alleged financial network and identify other entities involved in routing the proceeds of crime.

The latest arrest follows searches conducted by the ED across Pune, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Surat and Mehsana in Gujarat, which resulted in the seizure of incriminating documents and the freezing of nearly ₹9 Cr in cash held across multiple bank accounts.

The agency had also arrested Ram U Ramdhani, CEO of Edsom Fintech Pvt Ltd, in connection with the probe.

The arrest is part of ED’s broader clampdown on money laundering. Just days ago, the directorate launched investigations into alleged FEMA violations involving crypto platforms Mudrex and Saber.money as well as decentralised finance (DeFi) protocol Instadapp and its associated platform, Fluid, over alleged unauthorised cross-border fund transfers worth more than ₹4,940 Cr.

Prior to this in June this year, the ED had also searched six premises linked to five platforms, namely Transak, Carret, Xpat, Onramp.money and Onmeta, over alleged unauthorised cross-border crypto transfers.
